title: Research Bite #76: Fostering Teachers' Interpretations of Formative Assessment Results Using Clustered Heatmaps September 14, 2026
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.substack.com), discussing Bez, Wurster, Tomasik & Merk,
summary: This Research Bite breaks down a two-study paper by Bez, Wurster, Tomasik and Merk testing whether 'clustered heatmaps' — colour-coded assessment grids reordered so students with similar answer patterns sit together — actually improve how teachers interpret formative assessment data. The paper's own headline finding is a mixed one: in Study 1, 202 trainee teachers using the clustered heatmap grouped students faster and more accurately than those given a plain randomly-ordered table, but in Study 2, with 262 experienced teachers using real classroom data, the clustered format offered no accuracy advantage and only a marginal time saving, suggesting the benefit is largest for teachers who don't already have their own routines for reading assessment data. The paper's most important finding, however, cuts against display design altogether: researchers built in a pattern where students got a question wrong purely because of its format rather than a content gap, and virtually no teacher — regardless of which display they used — noticed it, leading the authors to conclude that visualization has a real ceiling once interpreting a pattern actually requires subject and question-level knowledge. Barton's own framing pulls the practical lesson forward for working teachers: before reteaching a whole topic because a question came back red on a grid, check whether the question's wording or format, not the underlying content, is actually what tripped students up, since a differently formatted question that assesses the same skill might reveal students already understand it.
points: The paper's own key limitation, stated directly by its authors: 'visualisations can come to a limit when content or context knowledge is needed to notice and interpret patterns in visualised data' — nearly no trainee teacher spotted a built-in question-format artifact, regardless of display.

Clustered heatmaps helped trainee teachers (202 participants) group students faster and more accurately than a plain random-order table, but showed no accuracy advantage for 262 experienced teachers using real classroom data in Study 2.

Barton's practical takeaway for teachers: before reteaching a whole topic because a question came back red on an assessment grid, check whether the question's wording or format — not the underlying content — is what actually tripped students up.
The authors explicitly warn against turning any of this into fixed ability groups, noting research shows downsides for lower-attaining and disadvantaged students from static grouping.
quotes: In Study 1, 202 trainee teachers using it grouped students more accurately and faster, and wrote better learning goals, than those given a plain table in random order. In Study 2, 262 experienced teachers compared it with a colour-coded grid in alphabetical order, using real classroom results. Here, accuracy was no better, and the time saving was small.

The researchers built a pattern into their made-up results. The lowest-attaining group could identify nouns, verbs and adjectives when ticking the right word type from a list, yet got the same content wrong when asked to underline or circle the word. Very few trainee teachers noticed this, and seeing the results as a heatmap made no difference.

The result that nearly none of the pre-service teachers noticed this pattern in the assessment results regardless of whether they saw the data displayed in a table or in a clustered heatmap suggests that visualisations can come to a limit when content or context knowledge is needed to notice and interpret patterns in visualised data.

When results show a class struggling on one question, check how that question was asked before you reteach the whole topic. In this study, very few trainee teachers noticed students failing purely because of a question's format, and a clearer display of the results made no difference.
The authors suggest experienced teachers have routines built around the layouts they already know, and an unfamiliar one can get in the way.
